title_short: Youssef · I Also Am to Blame
headline: A retired diplomat admits governments, himself included, did not listen to civil society enough.
story: Youssef spent decades on peace in the Middle East. His honest lesson: governments, and he too, did not listen to civil society as much as they should. Success is rare. Only people ready to fail again and again should do this work.

People move by their interests, so you find a way for them to work together. Young people must be at the table, even without a long CV. And civil society is on the ground: it knows things governments do not. Humble, wise, hopeful.

transcript:
Auto-transcript of FX6_LVH_6399.MXF (Youssef, Brussels, 15 Sep 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Speaker labels are often wrong. Interviewer lines: 00:15, 01:44-01:53, 02:47-03:13, 04:58-05:07, 07:02. Some of his own lines are labelled "Interviewer" (02:08, 02:31, 03:49, 04:17, 04:34).
[00:15] Interviewer: Could you tell us about your work in Egypt and the most significant lesson you've learned?
[00:25] My work is not in Egypt.
[00:31] I've been working over the last few decades to try to see how peace can be achieved in
[00:38] the Middle East and throughout this period I worked on different conflicts.
[00:44] I worked on Iraq reconciliation, Lebanon reconciliation, more recently I've been working on the situation
[00:52] in Yemen, the war against Iran, the situation in Sudan and of course the Arab-Israeli conflict
[01:00] and the Palestinian-Israeli conflict is the one that I've been focusing on most for many many years.
[01:07] Now what did I learn?
[01:09] Well I learned that success in this area is very rare and far apart and it is very difficult
[01:19] to achieve this success so for those who think that success is easy I think they should look
[01:25] But those who are ready to fail time and again perhaps this is where they should focus their efforts.
[01:38] Lots of different people for example with the Arab League, a big coalition of governments,
[01:44] Interviewer: what is the one thing that you have learned about in terms of working with diverse and big groups of governments and people?
[01:55] Well at the end of the day countries, groups, people are moved by their interests and we
[02:08] have to see how to accommodate the interests of different countries, groups, people in
[02:16] a manner that would allow them to work together rather than fight each other.
[02:23] This is easier said than done because always there are those who want to achieve more than
[02:31] what they deserve and then the burden is on those who are trying to help to see how a
[02:39] balance can be achieved between those who are fighting each other or those who are competing
[02:44] against each other to achieve different objectives.
[02:47] Interviewer: You've worked a lot on youth roles and attitudes and I wonder what you think about the role of young people and if there are any specific contexts within which you've worked where you really want to highlight the role that they played or maybe the role that you think they can or should play in Israel and Palestine?
[03:16] Well the role of young people is crucial in many places particularly in the Middle East
[03:23] because the average age in the Middle East is quite low.
[03:28] The number and percentage of youth in the vast majority of the countries in the region
[03:34] are more than a majority so we have to cater to their needs and their interests.
[03:41] Of course it is not easy because when we deal with governments it's very easy because you
[03:49] have official channels and when you deal with civil society it's also easy because
[03:54] there are organizations but then when you deal with youth it becomes more difficult
[03:59] because choosing what kind of youth you want and how they are chosen is a key issue.
[04:06] But then they are young, they don't have a long CV where you can judge them but then
[04:11] you still have to include them and this is the challenge that faces different people
[04:17] who want to be inclusive and want to have youth included in the effort that they are
[04:25] undergoing but find difficulty to achieve this objective.
[04:29] But this does not mean that we can give up because now as a result of technology things
[04:34] have become somewhat easier and I think those who are active and willing to participate
[04:41] from the young people have to be listened to particularly by old people because now
[04:47] the world has changed to an extent that requires us to take into account their needs much more
[04:54] than we have been doing for many decades.
[04:58] Interviewer: Do you see the role of Israeli and Palestinian civil society in shaping or taking part in the peace process from your position as diplomat?
[05:08] Well, I have been retired for a number of years and for a very long time I've been
[05:15] working on all kinds of activities both within government and within regional organizations
[05:24] and otherwise and the role of civil society is quite critical.
[05:31] The problem is that sadly governments and I also am to blame for that when I was in
[05:41] official positions, we did not listen to civil society as much as we should.
[05:47] But also not in defense of what we were doing, in many instances the situation dealt with
[05:57] all kinds of very confidential information that was not available to civil society and
[06:04] it couldn't be available to civil society.
[06:07] This made them at a disadvantage.
[06:10] Had they known some of this information they could have been much more helpful but sadly
[06:16] this is not always the case.
[06:18] So the question of confidentiality and secrecy of some of the efforts that are always ongoing
[06:24] in relation to conflict resolution sometimes prevents civil society from playing the role
[06:29] that they can play in a more effective way.
[06:32] But still at the end of the day civil society is on the ground.
[06:38] They know things that governments don't in relation to the level of hate speech for example,
[06:45] rhetoric becoming more on the extreme, the kind of difficulties on the ground in relation
[06:51] to violations of commitments and so on.
[06:54] Many of these things may not necessarily reach governments with the clarity that is reached
[07:01] by civil society.
[07:02] Interviewer: Can I ask one more question?
[07:19]-[09:46] (a question and answer on regional politics: out of this cut by design)
